hook: The general whose Art of War is still read by soldiers, coaches and business leaders.

pages.x: Sun Wu, honoured as Sun Tzu, "Master Sun", lived in the 6th century BC, when China was split into warring states. Tradition says he came from the state of Qi and served King Helu of Wu, in the south-east. Some historians doubt that he really existed.

To test him, King Helu asked whether he could drill even the palace women. Sun Tzu split 180 of them into two companies, led by the king's two favourite concubines. When they giggled at his orders, he had both favourites executed, despite the king's pleas. After that, the women drilled perfectly.
With his advice the small state of Wu beat Chu, its huge neighbour, at the Battle of Boju in 506 BC, and captured its capital. It was one of the most famous victories of the age.

His book, The Art of War, has 13 short chapters on planning, ground, spies and surprise. "All warfare is based on deception." "Know your enemy and know yourself, and in a hundred battles you will never be in danger." Its central idea: the greatest victory is the one won without fighting.

In 1972 archaeologists opening a Han dynasty tomb in Shandong found a copy of The Art of War written on bamboo strips, over 2,000 years old. Beside it lay a book on war by Sun Bin, his descendant, which had been lost for more than a thousand years.

The Art of War is the oldest and most famous book on strategy in the world. Its lessons on knowing yourself, outthinking an opponent and winning without a fight are studied by generals, business leaders and coaches.
pts: Taught that the best victory needs no battle
